notes.claim: Forces on one object balance when their sum is zero; with no net force an object stays at rest or keeps a constant velocity.
In a two-leg sling each leg tension has a vertical part that carries the load; the two vertical parts together must equal the weight, so each leg pulls harder than half the weight.
The load in each sling leg increases as the angle between the legs increases, and low angles are called extremely hazardous.
The extra tension appears without any extra load being lifted, and the sling itself is no weaker: only the force in each leg grows.
Load angle factors show the rise: leg tension times 1.000 at 90 degrees, 1.155 at 60, 1.414 at 45 and 2.000 at 30, with the angle measured from horizontal (some calculators use vertical).
Static friction matches the push up to a limit, F = μN; once the object slides, kinetic friction is a little smaller, so it is easier to keep it moving than to start it. For lesson i1's crate.
Lubrication makes both the static and the kinetic coefficient of friction considerably smaller. For lesson i1's crate.

sources.quote: For loads being lifted up- ward, as examined in this article, the angle of loading is the acute angle be- tween the sling leg and the horizontal plane.

sources.title: 5.2 Newton's First Law - University Physics Volume 1 | OpenStax — OpenStax
sources.quote: A body at rest remains at rest or, if in motion, remains in motion at constant velocity unless acted on by a net external force.

sources.title: 4.2 Newton's First Law of Motion: Inertia - Physics | OpenStax — OpenStax
sources.quote: According to Newton’s first law of motion, any object moving at constant velocity has no net external force acting upon it, which means that the sum of the forces acting on the object must be zero.

sources.quote: Once in motion, it is easier to keep it in motion than it was to get it started, indicating that the kinetic frictional force is less than the static frictional force.
